                                     PROJECT NO. 58777


 TRIENNIAL RELIABILITY                              §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 ASSESSMENT FOR THE ERCOT                                              OF TEXAS
                                                    §
 REGION UNDER § 25.508


               TEXAS PUBLIC POWER ASSOCIATION’S RESPONSE TO
                         QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT


       The Texas Public Power Association (TPPA) appreciates the opportunity to respond to the
questions for comment issued by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) staff
relating to the triennial reliability assessment for the Electric Reliability Council of Texas
(ERCOT) region under § 25.508. These comments are submitted on behalf of TPPA and do not
necessarily reflect the opinions of any individual TPPA member.

       Formed in 1978, TPPA is the statewide association for the 72 municipally owned utilities
(MOUs) in Texas. TPPA membership also includes several electric cooperatives and joint action
agencies, as well as the Lower Colorado River Authority. TPPA members serve urban, suburban,
and rural Texas and vary in size from large, vertically-integrated utilities to relatively small
distribution-only systems. We are proud to serve approximately 5.1 million Texans across the state.
Most of our members operate within the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region,
though several are located within either the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) or Midcontinent
Independent System Operator (MISO) region. MOUs offer a long track record of stability, and we
serve an essential role in providing secure and reliable power to the wholesale electricity markets
in these regions, including ERCOT. Many of our member systems have been providing stable and
reliable electric service to communities in Texas for over 100 years, and collectively, our members
provide more than 13,000 MW of generation and maintain more than 8,500 miles of high-voltage
transmission assets or more than 15% of the transmission in ERCOT.

       On January 30, the Commission issued questions for comment, seeking comments by
March 2. These responses are timely filed.




TPPA Comments                                                                         Page 1 of 12
                         I.      General Comments and Recommendations
1. At the July 25, 2024 open meeting, the Commission approved setting the CONE at
   $140,000/MW-year for planning purposes in the ERCOT region, including the triennial
   reliability assessment. Based on stakeholder feedback, ERCOT has proposed a plan for
   updating this CONE value.
       a. Does CONE need to be updated for the 2026 reliability standard assessment? Why or
            why not?

       TPPA recognizes that updating the CONE for the 2026 reliability standard assessment may
be appropriate, particularly given evolving market conditions and stakeholder interest in ensuring
planning assumptions remain current. If the Commission determines that an updated CONE value
would improve the analytical foundation of the reliability assessment, TPPA does not oppose
undertaking such an update.

       However, TPPA emphasizes that any effort to revise CONE must be conducted with
careful attention to process, timelines, and stakeholder participation. The triennial reliability
assessment is a foundational analysis that informs significant policy and market decisions. It is
therefore critical that stakeholders are provided adequate time and opportunity to review proposed
methodologies, underlying data, and resulting values, and to provide meaningful and substantive
feedback.

       CONE is a planning construct, not a precise representation of actual project costs faced by
individual developers. As such, the incremental benefit of refining the CONE estimate must be
balanced against the risks associated with compressed timelines, reduced transparency, or limited
stakeholder engagement. Updating CONE without sufficient time for review and discussion could
undermine confidence in the results of the reliability assessment and limit its usefulness to the
Commission and market participants.

       Accordingly, TPPA urges the Commission to ensure that, if CONE is updated for the 2026
reliability standard assessment, the process allows for robust stakeholder input and does not unduly
delay the assessment or constrain stakeholders’ ability to provide substantial feedback on both the
assumptions and outcomes of the reliability assessment analysis.




TPPA Comments                                                                          Page 2 of 12
        b. If the Commission considers an updated CONE value, are the scope and list of tasks
           proposed by Brattle and Sargent & Lundy in ERCOT's January 15, 2026 filing an
           acceptable method to update the calculations? If not, please provide recommended
           modifications to their approach.

       If the Commission determines that an updated CONE value is necessary, TPPA
recommends that any such update be narrowly tailored and grounded primarily in ERCOT-specific
data. CONE should reflect conditions relevant to the ERCOT market, including local construction
costs, interconnection practices, regulatory requirements, and resource characteristics, rather than
relying heavily on data or assumptions drawn from other regions of the country with different
market structures and cost drivers.



2. ERCOT has requested the Commission consider whether the load forecasts used in this study
   should align with the one that will be generated through the 2026 RTP compliance plan
   described in the Commission's rulemaking in Project No. 58480. ERCOT acknowledges that
   an updated load forecast that aligns with that compliance plan could be ready by April or May
   2026, which would push back the timeline of the reliability assessment by at least a month.
       a. Should the Commission approve updating the load forecast used in the 2026 reliability
           assessment to align with the compliance plan being considered in Project No. 58480,
           even if it will delay work on the reliability assessment?

       TPPA supports the use of a single, consistent load forecast across ERCOT planning studies
and agrees, as a general matter, that the load forecast used for the 2026 reliability assessment
should align with the forecast developed through the 2026 RTP compliance plan. At the same time,
TPPA emphasizes that the benefits of forecast alignment must be balanced against the need to
preserve reasonable timelines and meaningful stakeholder engagement. ERCOT has indicated that
a load forecast aligned with the RTP compliance plan may not be available until April or May
2026, which would delay completion of the reliability assessment. TPPA is concerned that such a
delay could compress the timeframe available for stakeholders and the Commission to review the
assessment results, assess their implications, and consider whether any market or regulatory
changes are warranted.



TPPA Comments                                                                          Page 3 of 12
        Accordingly, while TPPA prefers use of the RTP compliance plan load forecast and
supports moving toward a single forecast framework for future planning efforts, TPPA urges the
Commission to ensure that any decision to delay the reliability assessment does not limit
stakeholders’ ability to provide substantial feedback on the results. If alignment with the RTP
forecast would materially constrain review and deliberation, TPPA recommends that the
Commission carefully weigh whether the incremental benefit of alignment outweighs the
procedural costs.

       Regardless of the process outcome for this iteration of the reliability assessment, TPPA
supports efforts to better align development timelines for load forecasts and planning studies so
that a common load forecast is used across both resource adequacy and transmission planning to
improve consistency, transparency, and comparability of results and reduce the risk of conflicting
signals to policymakers and market participants.



       b. What other considerations should the Commission make regarding the load forecast
           used for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years?

       TPPA believes it is vital that the forecast account for the responsiveness of large loads
during periods of scarcity conditions and high prices, whether that responsiveness is voluntary or
mandatory. TPPA acknowledges that ERCOT’s list of assumptions includes a variable related to
price responsive demand and the 4CP program. However, TPPA does not believe this category, as
described in ERCOT’s filing, adequately captures the extent to which the recent influx of large
loads is unlikely to impact the bulk power system during extreme weather events and periods of
energy scarcity or reliability events. In practice, many large loads are expected to curtail or
otherwise reduce their net impact on the system during these conditions.



3. ERCOT proposed using the December 2025 Capacity, Demand, and Reserves (CDR) Report
   to create the base portfolio for evaluating the bulk power system in 2026 and 2029. This
   includes resource additions and retirements.




TPPA Comments                                                                        Page 4 of 12
        a. Does the generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report adequately capture
           the resource mix in both 2026 and 2029? If not, what additional assumptions should be
           made about resource additions and retirements?

       At this time, TPPA does not offer a response.



4. Based on information provided by the transmission operators, ERCOT proposed using 13,988
   MW as the magnitude criterion of the reliability standard for the 2026 simulation year. For the
   2029 simulation year, ERCOT proposes scaling the 2026 magnitude value by the ratio of the
   75th percentile load forecast for 2029 to the 75th percentile load forecast for 2026, resulting
   in a magnitude value of 14,509 MW for the 2029 simulation year.
       a. Should the Commission use these values for the magnitude criterion in the 2026 and
           2029 simulation years? If not, what modifications to these values should be made?

       TPPA supports the use of 13,988 MW as the magnitude criterion for the 2026 simulation
year. This value is based on information provided by transmission operators and is consistent with
the assumptions and data available for that time horizon.

       TPPA notes that future load forecasts and associated magnitude assumptions should
appropriately reflect the expected responsiveness of load, including large loads, during scarcity
conditions. The implementation of the SB6 demand response framework assumes a level of load
flexibility that does not currently exist across all large loads and may not be realized uniformly by
2029. To the extent the 2029 magnitude criterion relies on load growth assumptions that do not
adequately account for demand response participation or curtailment behavior during reliability
events, the resulting magnitude value may overstate system stress.



5. ERCOT proposed using the EIA' s 2025 Annual Energy Outlook and EIA Form 923 data to
   determine the natural gas and coal prices for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years. This results
   in prices of $2.84/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.47/MMBtu for coal in 2026 and
   $3.16/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.41/MMBtu for coal in 2029.




TPPA Comments                                                                          Page 5 of 12
        a. Are these assumptions for fuel prices for the 2026/2029 simulation years reasonable?
           If not, what alternative sources of information should be considered to determine these
           fuels prices?
       b. Should any sensitivity analyses on these fuel prices be considered?

       TPPA believes that sensitivity analyses on fuel price assumptions may be appropriate,
particularly given the inherent uncertainty associated with projecting natural gas and coal prices
several years into the future. Fuel prices can materially affect dispatch outcomes, scarcity
conditions, and reliability metrics, and therefore warrant careful consideration.

       To the extent sensitivity analyses are performed, TPPA recommends that such analyses be
clearly defined, limited in scope, and designed to test the directional impact of higher and lower
fuel price scenarios rather than to predict precise future price levels. Sensitivity cases should be
structured to inform the Commission’s understanding of how robust the reliability assessment
results are to reasonable variations in fuel price assumptions.



6. For previous reliability assessments, ERCOT has treated all historical weather years as having
   equal probability. For this assessment, ERCOT proposed weighing recent years more heavily.
       a. Should the Commission consider not treating all historical weather years as having
           equal probability? If yes, do you agree with ERCOT's proposed weighting of weather
           years?

        Treating all weather years as equally likely can distort reliability outcomes by overstating
the likelihood of extreme events relative to more typical system conditions. TPPA is concerned
that weighting recent years more heavily, without sufficiently distinguishing between the severity
and rarity of the events that occurred in those years, may still overemphasize extreme outlier events
simply because they are recent.

       In particular, Winter Storm Uri in 2021 has been widely characterized as a once-in-100-
year event. Assigning the same probability weight to 2021 as to more moderate weather years,
such as the 2022 winter, would overrepresent the likelihood of extreme conditions and could lead
to inaccurate or misleading reliability assessment results.




TPPA Comments                                                                           Page 6 of 12
        b. If you have an alternative weighting methodology, please provide additional details on
           your proposal. Please include justification for why your approach is better than what
           ERCOT has proposed.

       TPPA recommends that historical weather years be weighted based on both the
extremeness of the weather conditions experienced during those years and the likelihood of those
extreme events recurring, rather than on recency alone. Under this approach, years characterized
by rare, extreme events would receive lower probability weights than years reflecting more typical
system conditions, consistent with their expected frequency.

       Weighting weather years based on event severity and recurrence likelihood would better
align the reliability assessment with realistic risk expectations and would avoid disproportionately
skewing results toward low-probability, high-impact events. TPPA believes this approach would
produce more balanced and informative reliability outcomes than a methodology that assigns equal
probability to all years or that relies primarily on recency-based weighting.



7. ERCOT proposed using the multi-area reliability and economic dispatch modeling capability
   in SERVM to assess resource adequacy on a zonal basis that would account for transmission
   constraints between defined transmission zones. ERCOT states that any results from this
   analysis would be informational and not used to determine compliance with the reliability
   standard.
       a. Should the Commission approve an assessment of reliability metrics at the zonal level,
           understanding that these results would be purely informational and not used to
           determine compliance with the reliability standard?

       TPPA does not believe the Commission should approve an assessment of reliability metrics
at the zonal level at this time. TPPA does not see a clear benefit to conducting this additional
analysis as part of the 2026 reliability assessment, particularly given that the results would be
purely informational and not used to determine compliance with the reliability standard.

       The reliability standard assessment process is new and still being developed. Introducing
additional layers of analysis, especially those that increase modeling complexity, creates additional
opportunities for confusion, stakeholder disagreement, and delay. TPPA is concerned that


TPPA Comments                                                                          Page 7 of 12
 incorporating a zonal-level assessment could divert time and resources away from completing the
core reliability standard analysis within a reasonable timeframe.



          b. If so, do you have any proposed modifications to the approach ERCOT has
             recommended?

          Given TPPA’s view that a zonal reliability assessment is not necessary at this stage, TPPA
does not propose modifications to ERCOT’s recommended approach. TPPA notes, however, that
much of the information that could be derived from a zonal reliability assessment appears
redundant with the objectives of ERCOT’s annual Regional Transmission Plan and, prospectively,
ERCOT’s batch transmission studies.

          At this time, TPPA believes that adding a zonal reliability analysis would provide limited
incremental value while increasing the risk of delays in completing the reliability assessment.
TPPA therefore recommends that the Commission focus on completing and refining the system-
wide reliability standard before considering additional informational analyses in future assessment
cycles.



8. ERCOT proposed modifying how the model accounts for the effectiveness of the Commission's
   weatherization rule 16 TAC § 25.55. Previously, it was estimated to reduce weather-related
   outages by 85%, however under ERCOT' s proposed approach, the rule' s effectiveness would
   decline during extreme temperatures
          a. Do you agree with ERCOT's recommendation to deviate from the 85% effectiveness for
             the weatherization rule?

          TPPA does not agree with ERCOT’s recommendation to reduce the assumed effectiveness
of the Commission’s weatherization rule, 16 TAC § 25.55, below 85% for extreme events.
Moreover, TPPA recommends that the assumed effectiveness of weatherization generally be set
higher, rather than trending lower, based on recent operational experience, perhaps as high as 95%
effectiveness.

          As demonstrated during Winter Storm Fern, the generation fleet and transmission
infrastructure performed well under winter weather conditions, with significantly fewer weather-

TPPA Comments                                                                          Page 8 of 12
 related outages than experienced in prior extreme events. This performance suggests that the
existing weatherization requirements, combined with industry compliance efforts, have materially
improved generator and transmission resilience.

       In reviewing Winter Storm Fern, at the January 29, 2026 open meeting, the Commission
raised the question of whether the weatherization requirements should be updated to require higher
standards. In response to the question regarding the potential need for more stringent requirements,
ERCOT indicated that such updates would be unnecessary, noting that entities are exceeding the
existing weatherization standards and that there is no evidence demonstrating that the current
requirements are ineffective for winter weather conditions affecting Texas.

       Given this recent performance and ERCOT’s own statements regarding compliance and
effectiveness, TPPA believes that the weatherization effectiveness factor should be set above 85%.
TPPA also does not believe it is appropriate to assume declining effectiveness of the
weatherization rule during extreme temperatures. Doing so would understate the demonstrated
reliability benefits of weatherization and could skew the results of the reliability assessment.



9. ERCOT has proposed assumptions for the outages:
       a. Are the assumptions for generation and ESR outage modeling reasonable? If not, what
           modifications do you propose?
       b. How should ERCOT treat planned transmission outages in the model?

       TPPA does not believe planned transmission outages should be included in the reliability
assessment model, which focuses on long-term planning horizons. Planned transmission outages
are expected to be managed through operational planning and coordination and, by their nature,
tend to create localized reliability issues rather than system-wide reliability events.

       The reliability standard assessment is intended to evaluate bulk power system adequacy on
a system-wide basis. Including planned transmission outages risks introducing local reliability
events into an analysis that is not designed to assess localized transmission constraints. Doing so
could distort the results of the assessment and detract from its intended purpose.

       Accordingly, TPPA recommends that planned transmission outages be excluded from the
modeling assumptions used in the reliability standard assessment.

TPPA Comments                                                                             Page 9 of 12
 10. Please provide comments and recommendations on any of the model input assumptions that
   Staff has not specifically flagged in previous questions.

       At this time, TPPA has concerns regarding several model input assumptions that have not
been specifically addressed in prior questions, particularly those related to ancillary services
procurement and operational practices in the later simulation years.

       First, it is unclear what ancillary service methodology will be assumed for the 2029
simulation year. At the Commission’s September 18, 2025, open meeting, the Commission
indicated that the current paradigm of conservative operations should be re-evaluated, with the
potential to move away from the paradigm entirely . Given this stated policy direction, assumptions
that rely on existing ancillary service frameworks or conservative operational practices may not
accurately reflect conditions in 2029.

       Second, there is significant uncertainty regarding the future role and procurement levels of
Dispatchable Reliability Reserve Service (DRRS). At this time, it is unclear how much DRRS
ERCOT will procure in 2029 and how that procurement will affect ERCOT’s Reliability Unit
Commitment (RUC) strategy. These uncertainties are further compounded by ERCOT’s recent
implementation of Real-Time Co-Optimization, after which operational practices and RUC
behavior remain in flux.

       Because ancillary service procurement levels and RUC strategies can materially affect
scarcity outcomes and reliability metrics, TPPA believes additional clarity and stakeholder input
are needed before these assumptions are finalized for use in the reliability assessment.




TPPA Comments                                                                        Page 10 of 12
                                       II.      Conclusion

       At this time, TPPA has no additional comments on the questions for comment.

       TPPA appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments. As always, TPPA looks
forward to working with the Commission, Commission Staff, and stakeholders on this important
discussion in the coming months.




Dated: March 2, 2026
                                            Respectfully,

                                            ____________________
                                            Mariah Benson
                                            Regulatory Affairs Manager
                                            Texas Public Power Association
                                            PO Box 82768
                                            Austin, Texas 78708
                                            (512) 472-5965
                                            mbenson@tppa.com




TPPA Comments                                                                  Page 11 of 12
                 Texas Public Power Association’s (TPPA) Executive Summary

•   TPPA supports updating CONE for the 2026 reliability standard assessment if the Commission
    determines it would improve the analytical foundation, but only if the update is conducted with
    sufficient time, transparency, and opportunity for meaningful stakeholder review and feedback, and
    does not limit opportunities for stakeholder feedback on the outcomes of the reliability assessment
    analysis.

•   If the Commission determines that CONE should be updated, TPPA recommends the update be
    narrowly tailored and based primarily on ERCOT-specific data.

•   TPPA supports use of a single, consistent load forecast across ERCOT planning studies and generally
    prefers that the 2026 reliability assessment align with the load forecast developed through the 2026
    RTP compliance plan.

•   TPPA urges the Commission to ensure that any decision to delay the reliability assessment to achieve
    load forecast alignment does not limit stakeholders’ ability to provide substantial feedback, and
    recommends weighing the incremental benefits of alignment against the associated procedural costs.

•   TPPA believes load forecasts must adequately account for the responsiveness of large loads during
    periods of scarcity and high prices, whether that responsiveness is voluntary or mandatory.

•   TPPA cautions that the SB6 demand response framework assumes a level of load flexibility that does
    not yet exist across all large loads and may not be uniformly realized in the 2029 load forecast, and
    that magnitude assumptions relying on load growth may fail to account for realistic demand response
    or curtailment behavior.

•   TPPA recommends that any fuel price sensitivity analyses be clearly defined and limited in scope,
    focusing on testing the directional impacts of higher and lower price scenarios rather than attempting
    to predict precise future price levels.

•   TPPA recommends weighting historical weather years based the severity of the weather conditions
    and the likelihood of such extreme events recurring, rather than on recency alone.

•   TPPA does not recommend a zonal-level analysis be completed because TPPA is concerned that
    resources spent on this assessment could detract from timely completion and thorough review of the
    system-wide reliability assessment analysis.

•   TPPA does not support reducing the assumed effectiveness of the Commission’s weatherization rule
    below 85% for extreme events and recommends that the assumed effectiveness generally be set
    higher, potentially as high as 95%, based on recent operational performance.

•   TPPA recommends that planned transmission outages be excluded from the reliability assessment
    model, as they primarily create localized reliability issues rather than system-wide events as measured
    under the reliability assessment.

•   TPPA recommends that the assumptions for the 2029 ancillary service procurement methodology,
    including DRRS, be clarified and subjected to meaningful stakeholder review before being finalized,
    as they can materially affect scarcity outcomes and reliability metrics.



TPPA Comments                                                                               Page 12 of 12

6. For previous reliability assessments, ERCOT has treated all historical weather years as having
   equal probability. For this assessment, ERCOT proposed w eighing recent years more heavily.
       a. Should the Commission consider not treating all historical weather years as having
           equal probability? Ifyes, do you agree with ERCOT's proposed weighting of weather
           years?

        Treating all weather years as equally likely can distort reliability outcomes by overstating
the likelihood of extreme events relative to more typical system conditions. TPPA is concerned
that weighting recent years more heavily, without sufficiently distinguishing between the severity
and rarity ofthe events that occurred in those years, may still overemphasize extreme outlier events
simply because they are recent.

       In particular, Winter Storm Uri in 2021 has been widely characterized as a once-in-100-
year event. Assigning the same probability weight to 2021 as to more moderate weather years,
such as the 2022 winter, would overrepresent the likelihood of extreme conditions and could lead
to inaccurate or misleading reliability assessment results.




TPPA Comments                                                                          Page 6 of 12
        b. Ifyou have an alternative weighting methodology, please provide additional details on
            your proposal. Please include justification for why your approach is better than what
            ERCOT has proposed.

       TPPA recommends that historical weather years be weighted based on both the
extremeness of the weather conditions experienced during those years and the likelihood of those
extreme events recurring, rather than on recency alone. Under this approach, years characterized
by rare, extreme events would receive lower probability weights than years reflecting more typical
system conditions, consistent with their expected frequency.

       Weighting weather years based on event severity and recurrence likelihood would better
align the reliability assessment with realistic risk expectations and would avoid disproportionately
skewing results toward low-probability, high-impact events. TPPA believes this approach would
produce more balanced and informative reliability outcomes than a methodology that assigns equal
probability to all years or that relies primarily on recency-based weighting.

9. ERCOT has proposed assumptions for the outages:
       a. Are the assumptions for generation and ESR outage modeling reasonable? Ifnot, w hat
           modifications do you propose?
       b. How should ERCOT treat planned transmission outages in the model?

        TPPA does not believe planned transmission outages should be included in the reliability
assessment model, which focuses on long-term planning horizons. Planned transmission outages
are expected to be managed through operational planning and coordination and, by their nature,
tend to create localized reliability issues rather than system-wide reliability events.

        The reliability standard assessment is intended to evaluate bulk power system adequacy on
a system-wide basis. Including planned transmission outages risks introducing local reliability
events into an analysis that is not designed to assess localized transmission constraints. Doing so
could distort the results of the assessment and detract from its intended purpose.

       Accordingly, TPPA recommends that planned transmission outages be excluded from the
modeling assumptions used in the reliability standard assessment.

potential to move away from the paradigm entirely . Given this stated policy direction, assumptions
that rely on existing ancillary service frameworks or conservative operational practices may not
accurately reflect conditions in 2029.

       Second, there is significant uncertainty regarding the future role and procurement levels of
Dispatchable Reliability Reserve Service (DRRS). At this time, it is unclear how much DRR S
ERCOT will procure in 2029 and how that procurement will affect ERCOT's Reliability Unit
Commitment (RUC) strategy. These uncertainties are further compounded by ERCOT' s recent
implementation of Real-Time Co-Optimization, after which operational practices and RUC
behavior remain in flux.

       Because ancillary service procurement levels and RUC strategies can materially affect
scarcity outcomes and reliability metrics, TPPA believes additional clarity and stakeholder input
are needed before these assumptions are finalized for use in the reliability assessment.

    that magnitude assumptions relying on load growth may fail to account for realistic demand response

    to predict precise future price levels.
